gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the '65W' in a universal adapter's name can come from only one USB-C port. On TESSAN's WTA07 and WTA09 only port C3 gives 65 W, and the other two USB-C ports and both USB-A ports give at most 15 W each, so a laptop plugged into the wrong port gets 15 W.
standout_why: I compared against packandporter.com, universaltraveladapter.net (a TESSAN-branded page), theitalyguides.com and NBC Select. All of them say that an adapter does not convert voltage and that devices need 100–240 V input. Pack & Porter also says a Swiss Type J socket takes a slim Type C plug but not a Schuko F, and that compact universal adapters are ungrounded. Pack & Porter gives only a total (about 30 W across all ports) for the Epicka TA-105C. NBC says it doesn't explain how the Epicka Pulse splits power between ports. None of these pages says which port gives the headline wattage or how little the other ports give.
decides: This confirms the plug choice and refines the charging advice. For a US traveller, the plug type and voltage are settled: a Type C adapter works for most of the continent, and a phone or laptop charger with a 100–240 V input is fine. What decides whether a USB-C laptop charges from the adapter alone is the wattage of each port, not the wattage on the box. The Ceptics CTU-9C ($9.99) has one socket that takes a US 2-prong or 3-prong cord, so the laptop's own charger can go there. With a TESSAN WTA07 ($42.99) or WTA09 ($27.99), the laptop must use port C3 because the other ports top out at 15 W. Hair tools need dual-voltage ratings: TESSAN's TC03 converter is capped at 250 W output.
